headings.title: Prepared settings do not become new defaults

html:
Prepared requests and queue admission

Preparing a request captures the settings and parameter references accepted for that request. Submitting it later must use that captured identity. A repeated HTTP request must not change the accepted configuration or start the same queue item twice. This guide describes that admission boundary; the follow-up queue separately owns continuation order and automatic advancement.

Implementation owners

Owner Responsibility
Request lifecycle Handles prepare/submit requests, selects the queue path, claims before launch and returns existing stream/trace links for recognized retries.
QueueSubmissions Resolves accepted policies, validates request digests and predecessor lineage, and supplies standalone SQLite capture/claim methods.
MemoryQueueSubmissions Implements active-controller capture, admission fences and queue claims in the runtime hub while rejecting SQL access.
Native RunStore Supplies the registered state owner, views and transaction boundary used by the queue adapter.

Constructing QueueSubmissions checks whether the current-run path already has a RAM owner. If so, it selects MemoryQueueSubmissions; otherwise it retains the standalone SQLite adapter. The shared interface does not open a second live SQL authority for the controller. Neither implementation starts a worker or advances queue order itself.

Accepted identity

flowchart LR Envelope[Typed prompt, conversation and Gateway/context selection] --> Digest[Canonical accepted-envelope digest] Explicit[Supplied policies and accepted behavior/capability authority] --> Digest Digest --> Binding[Queue ID, request ID and predecessor binding] Settings[Settings and scoped policy resolvers] --> Capture[Prepared policy rows keyed by request ID] Parameters[Transaction-owned Parameter Store] --> Snapshot[Accepted parameter snapshot] Capture --> Resolve[Submission resolves saved settings] Snapshot --> Resolve Binding --> Validate[Validate unchanged identity and predecessor] Resolve --> Validate Validate --> Admission[Request lifecycle admission] Admission --> Native[Native run state and execution ownership] Native --> Evidence[Trace and stream projections]

There are three related records: the binding identifies the accepted queue item, prepared rows retain its settings and parameters, and native state eventually owns execution. Trace/stream links expose observations about that request. A preparation trace alone does not establish that a worker started.

A queue binding associates queue_id, request_id, predecessor identity, snapshot_digest, claim state and eventual conversation identity. Companion prepared records retain accepted policies and parameter snapshots. The compact binding row itself does not contain the prompt body.

The digest comes from the validated request envelope and accepted behavior and capability authority. It includes the exact prompt, conversation, Gateway/context selection and supplied execution policies. Other accepted settings live in their prepared records; the digest is not a serialization of every stored bundle row. Attachment ordering remains meaningful. Missing and null conversation IDs have the same digest representation, while presentation labels do not confer authority.

Queued context accepts only the declared Gateway selection, Context references and Agent UI target. A Gateway ID and captured capability/permission policies are required. At most 16 Context IDs are accepted here. Unknown execution fields or invalid references fail with HTTP 422; a changed supplied digest fails with 409. The code recognizes historical digests containing the retired summarize_result switch only in the compatible carry-all case. It does not restore that switch as runtime behavior.

Capture before publication

flowchart TD Input[Validated prepare request] --> Fence[Read admission and conversation revisions] Fence --> Existing{Queue binding exists?} Existing -->|Yes| Match[Validate original digest and predecessor] Existing -->|No| Bundle[Capture accepted policies and parameter references] Bundle --> Publish[Commit complete bundle and queue binding] Match --> Trace[Create or reconcile preparation trace] Publish --> Trace Trace --> Prepared[Return prepared request identity] Prepared --> Validate[Validate same accepted identity on submit] Validate --> Claim[Atomically mark claimed before worker launch] Claim --> Caller[Caller owns execution admission and launch]

RAM preparation reads admission revision keys for settings, Gateways and parameters before resolving their values. It also reads conversation and deletion/tombstone state. Relevant concurrent changes conflict with the transaction and cause its capture callback to retry. Parameter references must come from the same hub; resolution uses its transaction view and does not record parameter usage at this boundary.

The complete policy bundle is captured before publishing a new queue binding. Otherwise subsequent lookups could mistake a partially built bundle for an existing prepared request. New queued RAM captures reserve admission capacity and associate the prepared request with its conversation. A candidate request ID is chosen outside the retryable callback, so transaction retries retain that identity.

The RAM adapter creates preparation trace state after the transaction commits. A failed trace projection can therefore leave an accepted bundle without its presentation record; an exact retry reuses the binding and retries the trace step. The standalone SQLite adapter uses an immediate transaction and performs its trace call within that transaction's lifetime. These are distinct implementation paths.

Active-controller capture sequence

sequenceDiagram participant R as Request lifecycle participant Q as RAM queue adapter participant H as Shared hub transaction participant T as Trace store R->>Q: Prepare typed queue envelope Q->>Q: Allocate candidate request ID outside retry callback loop Until a conflict-free publication or a rejected request Q->>H: Read settings, Gateway, parameter and conversation fences Q->>H: Resolve accepted digest and look up queue ID alt Existing queue binding Q->>H: Check digest and resolved predecessor identity H-->>Q: Original accepted binding else New queue binding Q->>H: Reserve admission capacity and check predecessor Q->>H: Capture complete policies and parameters Q->>H: Bind request owner and queue identity H-->>Q: Commit complete prepared bundle end end opt Binding remains unclaimed Q->>T: Create or reconcile preparation trace T-->>Q: Preparation observation end Q-->>R: Stable request ID, digest and claim state Note over Q,T: A trace failure after commit leaves the accepted binding intact

The surrounding HTTP preparation owner requires accepted legal terms, checks parameter resolution and rejects slash commands. Unresolved parameter references enter its held-request path. Its semaphore bounds preparation workers, and its queue lock serializes queued requests through that service instance. The RAM transaction still protects independent adapters and concurrent state edits.

Inside capture, policy resolvers use the transaction-local view. Relevant revision changes retry the callback with the same candidate request ID. A rejected callback publishes neither a partial bundle nor a binding. On a later exact retry, an existing binding retains its accepted settings; missing required rows are a conflict, not a request to recapture current defaults.

The policy bundle covers capability selection and ceilings, behavior effort, goal echo, context efficiency, ramble guard, Python correction, carry-forward, notebook reads, context recovery, prose generation, Task Contract mode/integrity and accepted controls, Context reads, parallelism, supervision, background work, dependency/resource scheduling, stop policy, redaction, runtime guards and their provenance/monitoring flag. Parameter bindings are captured alongside these rows. The digest covers the envelope described above, rather than every policy row.

Prepared settings do not become new defaults

Shared policy helpers distinguish three cases:

  • New ingress has no prepared identity, so it may resolve current defaults and permitted request overrides.
  • Existing prepared work requires its saved value. Missing required rows produce HTTP 409 instead of consulting a newer global setting.
  • Selected optional legacy fields have explicit compatibility behavior: missing context-recovery allowance becomes zero, notebook reads use product defaults, and carry-forward uses its normalized legacy default.

Explicit behavior-effort, capability-policy/selection or carry-forward values that conflict with accepted snapshots are rejected. Capture methods insert only absent rows. The Python entrypoint-correction field is filled only while its existing prepared behavior row still holds a null value.

The RAM implementation interns one identical capability snapshot to reduce retained memory. It still resolves and validates current authority for every new admission; the interned value is not an authorization cache. The standalone Task Contract capture explicitly adds a model-routing snapshot to its accepted policy. The RAM override stores the controls policy returned by accepted_policy_snapshot directly; these two capture bodies should not be assumed byte-for-byte equivalent.

Claim and retry behavior

Submission requires the prepared request ID and its original queue-submission identity. Validation compares the digest and resolves predecessor aliases through same-task continuation links. Cyclic or unverifiable lineage conflicts with 409.

When native predecessor state exists, this binding layer rejects interrupted runs, unknown operations and states still active or waiting. It accepts the terminal states completed, answered, cancelled and failed. When native state is absent, it checks retained trace/current-run interruption evidence; absence alone is not proof of successful completion. Queue advancement owners can impose stricter requirements. In particular, automatic follow-up dispatch requires a successful head as described in the follow-up guide.

Claiming revalidates the binding and atomically records claimed and conversation identity before the request lifecycle starts a worker. A second claim returns 409. If the process stops after claim but before launch evidence appears, the binding does not authorize another launch.

Replay returns the original request, stream and trace links only when native run state or submitted trace timing establishes prior admission. A claimed row without either observation returns 409 with an unverified-outcome diagnostic. Operators should reconcile that original request through normal task/run diagnostics rather than recreate its identity. This module has no TTL or routine that resets a claim. Runtime persistence and recovery remain owned by the existing state system.

Predecessor reconciliation

flowchart TD Start[Resolve supplied and saved predecessor anchors] --> Lineage[Follow request aliases and same-task continuations] Lineage --> Cycle{Repeated lineage identity?} Cycle -->|Yes| Conflict[HTTP 409] Cycle -->|No| Match{Resolved anchors match?} Match -->|No| Conflict Match -->|Yes| Claimed{Binding already claimed?} Claimed -->|Yes| Replay[Reconcile original request without another claim] Claimed -->|No| State{Native predecessor state exists?} State -->|Yes| Unsafe{Interrupted or unknown operations?} Unsafe -->|Yes| Conflict Unsafe -->|No| Terminal{Completed, answered, cancelled or failed?} Terminal -->|No| Conflict Terminal -->|Yes| Eligible[Binding-level predecessor check passes] State -->|No| Trace[Read retained trace and current-run interruption evidence] Trace --> Interrupted{Interruption retained?} Interrupted -->|Yes| Conflict Interrupted -->|No| Eligible Eligible --> More[Caller still enforces capacity and execution authority]

For a new preparation there is no saved anchor to compare; the adapter directly checks the supplied predecessor. The RAM absence path reads trace status and related current-run projections in the same transaction. It does not infer a successful outcome from missing native state. These binding checks are separate from the server-owned conversation task coordinator and automatic follow-up success requirements.

Submission, claim and replay sequence

sequenceDiagram participant U as Request client participant R as Request lifecycle participant Q as Queue binding owner participant E as Trace and native evidence participant W as Runtime worker U->>R: Submit prepared ID and original queue envelope R->>Q: Read saved parameters and validate binding under queue lock alt Binding already claimed R->>E: Resolve original native state or submitted trace timing alt Prior admission is observable E-->>R: Original request identity R-->>U: Original request, stream and trace links else Neither observation exists R-->>U: HTTP 409 unverified outcome end else Binding is unclaimed R->>R: Claim trace and perform model/Gateway preflight R->>R: Resolve effective authority and conversation, then check capacity R->>Q: Revalidate and atomically claim queue binding Q-->>R: Claimed identity and conversation recorded R->>E: Publish current-run and session projections R->>W: Start the runtime worker R-->>U: Request, stream and trace links end Note over R,W: Claim and worker launch are separate boundaries

The client-facing preparation endpoint may return links for an already claimed binding without proving execution. Submission replay has the stricter evidence check shown above. Even that evidence establishes prior admission, not successful completion: the caller must inspect the original run's outcome.

The local queue lock covers validation through submission in one service instance; the binding's atomic claim protects independent contenders. A competing claim fails with 409. Earlier preflight or later projection/launch failures can leave trace or other records behind; this sequence is not one cross-store rollback. The binding owner never resets claimed to launch again. The detailed admission and diagnostic paths belong to the request lifecycle, while retained server-owned task attempts belong to the conversation coordinator.

Validation scope

Queue submission fixtures exercise prepare/submit identity, repeated requests and predecessor handling. RAM fixtures exercise concurrent capture/claim, restart and immutable snapshots with runtime SQLite denied. They use local fixtures, not production model workloads. Current outcomes and baseline failures are recorded in the documentation review status.
